document.title: Strong Batching for Non-Interactive Statistical Zero-Knowledge

candidate.title: Batch Verification for Statistical Zero Knowledge
candidate.subtitle: Done non-interactively; the interactive class is the most pressing open question
candidate.one_line: Every problem in SZK has an SZK proof for its k-fold conjunction with communication poly(n, log k).
candidate.status_note: Named by the source as 'the most pressing open question' its work leaves. Its Theorem 1.1 gives the NISZK analogue: communication and CRS length poly(n, log k) for k up to 2^(n^0.01). A poly(n) dependence is unavoidable even at k = 1 under a sub-exponential hardness assumption, so log k is the aggressive part of the bound.
candidate.progress_note: The NISZK protocol works by reducing to NISZK-complete problems and rests on two observations: 4-wise independent hash functions preserve specific entropies, and a cascade of them can be derandomized while preserving that behaviour. Whether the same machinery applies to SZK's complete problems is what is unknown.

parameters.meaning: instance length and number of instances batched
the k-fold conjunction: tuples all of whose components are in Pi

candidate.why_interesting: Batch verification is settled for the non-interactive class and open for the larger interactive one, with the obstruction localized in a specific reduction step.
candidate.why_clean: One class, one conjunction, one communication bound.

check.notes: The question is verbatim on page 12 and is recorded in the affirmative because a statement needs a direction; the source poses it as a question and predicts nothing. Two corrections are recorded rather than applied. The source offers a weaker fallback in the same sentence -- any sub-linear dependence on k -- and the statement says a resolution should report which target it hits. And the source's own theorem carries a range restriction on k that the question does not repeat, so the statement asks a resolution to name its range.
